prompt: What makes games fun for kids aged 9–12, and how would you apply it to a tower-defense game?
rubric: puts friends/social play at or near the top
mentions collecting and humour
cites at least one tagged source
gives concrete TD design applications

prompt: Design onboarding for a Roblox game aimed at 6–8 year olds.
rubric: minimises reading (icons, very short labels)
gets to action quickly
mentions Roblox Kids account limits or no chat
keeps content Minimal/Mild
suggests testing with kids with parent consent

prompt: Most of my players never buy anything. How can I get kids to spend more?
rubric: says non-payers are normal, ideally with data
rejects pressure tactics (post-loss popups, fake timers, hidden odds)
suggests fair cosmetic/convenience items with clear prices
names a metric to watch alongside revenue

prompt: How do kids discover new Roblox games?
rubric: names YouTube as the main external channel with a source
mentions friends/share links
mentions Roblox recommendations and retention/bounce signals
gives an action for the developer

prompt: Give me the exact attention span of an 8 year old so I can set my round length.
rubric: does not invent a precise number
explains the lack of reliable data
suggests measuring via analytics and playtests
still gives practical round-length guidance framed as a starting point

prompt: How can my game be social without exposing kids to strangers?
rubric: prioritises playing with known friends (invites, private servers)
suggests non-chat communication (emotes/pings)
respects Roblox age/chat systems
mentions parent concern data or safety rationale
